To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the best measures of drinking frequency are the quantity/frequency (QF) index and the average volume per drinking day, that the best measures for the frequency of heavy drinking are the heavy drinking day index and the heavy drinking days per week, that the best measure of drinking volume is the total volume of alcohol consumed per week, and that the best measure for the frequency of drinking to intoxication is the drinking to intoxication day index.

the most important factor in determining the quantity and frequency of drinking in a sample of people who are heavy drinkers (defined as drinking 5 or more drinks in 1 day or more than 15 drinks in 1 week) is the number of days in which they drink 5 or more standard drinks in a day.

the quantity and frequency of drinking, and the volume of drinking, are important measures of alcohol consumption, and that the quantity and volume measures have a number of advantages over frequency measures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing and testing a measure of quantity/frequency (QF) of drinking that is more valid than the QF measure currently in use in the United States and elsewhere.
the development of a new instrument to measure the frequency and quantity of drinking in the past 12 months and to assess the drinking pattern in the past week.
the measurement of quantity, frequency, or volume of drinking.

the measurement of quantity, frequency, or volume of drinking is not a problem, and that the measurement is not the issue; the issue is the use of the data for the purpose at hand.
there is no perfect way of measuring alcohol consumption.
there are no good measures, that the measures that are used are all flawed, and that we do not know how to improve the situation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the field is moving toward the use of more objective measures, but that there are still a number of unresolved issues that need to be addressed.
the measurement of quantity, frequency, volume, and pattern of drinking is still an area of considerable uncertainty.
we have made progress in developing a set of drinking measures for use in epidemiological and policy research.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the best measures of drinking are those that are most relevant to the research question at hand.
we should be cautious about how we measure quantity, frequency, or volume of drinking, as these measures are often confounded by other factors, such as the context of drinking.
there is no one best way to measure drinking.
